thesis: Unsloth 0.1.909 makes DeepSeek V4.1 run locally on a 128 GB machine, but fine-tuning V4.1 itself has no shipped recipe -- what you actually train tonight is the stock Unsloth QLoRA flow on an open model that fits your card.
explanation_path: Start with what actually landed yesterday: a beta release whose headline is that a 552B-parameter open-weight model now runs on a 128 GB machine, because its 196B Engram lookup table can sit on SSD while rows load on demand. Establish what the model is -- a mixture of experts where about 16B parameters fire per token -- before touching fine-tuning, because the active-parameter number is exactly what makes people misjudge the memory bill. Then the honest turn: read the release and its guide closely and V4.1 support is run support; no V4.1 fine-tuning recipe, notebook or 4-bit training checkpoint shipped, and the stock Unsloth QLoRA recipe is unchanged, its one-string model swap reaching only models with published 4-bit checkpoints. Land the payoff on what the viewer does tonight: run the stock recipe end to end on a model that fits -- load in 4-bit, attach LoRA adapters, train on a question-answer dataset, save a small adapter, export to GGUF -- and note the gotcha that V4.1 ships no Jinja chat template at all. Close on why V4.1 still matters to them: it is the model they run beside the model they train, and if a V4.1 training path lands, this same recipe inherits it.

claims.claim: Unsloth shipped release v0.1.909-beta, titled DeepSeek-V4.1 & FLUX-3, on 2026-10-19, and its headline is that DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 now runs locally in Unsloth.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 has 552B parameters plus 196B in its Engram table, about 16B active, and 1M tokens of context, and with the Engram table left on SSD it runs in about 125 GB of memory at 1-bit, or 300 GB at 4-bit.
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 scores 42.3 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, up from 31.2 for the earlier DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.
The release's Training section ships no DeepSeek-V4.1 fine-tuning recipe; its training news is generic multi-GPU FSDP2 for LoRA, QLoRA and full fine-tuning.
Unsloth's official DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash guide is a run-and-serve guide, and its only training pointer tells you to fine-tune other models.
claims.source_title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Run Locally Guide | Unsloth Documentation

claims.claim: The unslothai/notebooks catalog of 250+ fine-tuning notebooks lists no DeepSeek-V4 or V4.1 fine-tuning notebook; its only DeepSeek entries are DeepSeek R1 0528 Qwen3 (8B).
claims.source_title: unslothai/notebooks: 250+ Fine-tuning & RL Notebooks for text, vision, audio, embedding, TTS models.

claims.claim: DeepSeek's official model card says this release ships no Jinja-format chat template, replacing it with a Python reference implementation and the deepseek-recipe Rust toolkit.

In the stock Unsloth recipe you swap models by changing one string to a 4-bit checkpoint name such as unsloth/llama-3.1-8b-unsloth-bnb-4bit, and load_in_4bit = True enables 4-bit quantization that reduces memory use 4x for fine-tuning.
Unsloth says you can fine-tune or do RL for free on Colab, Kaggle, or locally with just 3GB VRAM by using its notebooks.

analogy_candidates.vehicle: A library with a basement archive
analogy_candidates.mapping: The 196B Engram table is the reference shelf that stays in the basement (on SSD); a clerk pages in only the few rows each token needs, so the reading room stays small.
analogy_candidates.limit: It makes the model sound streamable onto any PC, but the non-Engram weights alone still need 122.4 GB (UD-IQ1_S), so a 24 GB card never qualifies.

analogy_candidates.vehicle: A hospital with 552B staff and about 16B on shift per patient
analogy_candidates.mapping: Mixture of experts routes each token to a few specialists, so the compute per token feels small while the whole staff stays on the payroll, in memory.
analogy_candidates.limit: Memory follows the full headcount, not the shift roster -- Unsloth's tables price 1-bit at 128–145 GB of total memory -- so 16B active never becomes a 16B memory bill.

analogy_candidates.vehicle: A vinyl wrap on a car
analogy_candidates.mapping: LoRA trains thin added matrices instead of repainting the whole body -- Unsloth says you optimize about 1% of weights -- and ships as a small wrap you reuse on the same chassis.
analogy_candidates.limit: The wrap still needs the entire car underneath; you cannot wrap a 552B-parameter chassis that does not fit in your garage.

misconceptions.myth: DeepSeek V4.1 has only about 16B active parameters, so it should fit in memory like a 16B model.
misconceptions.reality: Memory is set by the whole checkpoint, not the active slice: Unsloth's requirement table puts the 1-bit quant at 128–145 GB of total memory, because every expert sits in RAM or VRAM even though only about 16B run per token (claims 2 and 8).

misconceptions.myth: Unsloth 0.1.909's DeepSeek-V4.1 support means you can fine-tune V4.1 tonight by changing one flag in the stock recipe.
misconceptions.reality: The release and its guide cover running, not training: no V4.1 fine-tuning recipe, notebook or 4-bit training checkpoint shipped, and the stock recipe's one-string model swap only reaches models with published 4-bit checkpoints (claims 4, 5, 6 and 8).

glossary.definition: Continuing to train a downloaded model on your own examples so it fits your task or voice.
Thin trainable matrices attached to a frozen model so you train a sliver of the weights instead of all of them.
LoRA done on a 4-bit compressed copy of the model, which cuts training memory by about 4x.
Compressing model weights to roughly 4 bits each so they take about a quarter of the memory, at some accuracy cost.
The small trained file (Unsloth shows it around 100 MB) you save and later load on top of the unchanged base model.
The single-file model format that llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio run, and the format Unsloth exports for local use.
A model built from many specialist blocks where a router activates only a few of them for each token.
The slice of the model actually computed for each token -- about 16B in DeepSeek V4.1 -- which is not the memory footprint.
DeepSeek V4.1's 196B-parameter n-gram lookup memory, which can sit on SSD while a few rows load on demand.
The per-model formatting rules that wrap your text into the exact prompt shape the model was trained on.
Memory a machine shares between CPU and GPU, like a 128 GB DGX Spark, so the model draws from one pool.

unverified: No fetched page states the memory or time a QLoRA fine-tune of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 would need, or that Unsloth supports training it at all.
No community report of anyone fine-tuning V4.1 in the first 24 hours was found or corroborated by a tier 1-3 page.
Whether the missing Jinja chat template blocks standard LoRA training pipelines for V4.1 is inference from the model card, not a documented statement.
Tokens per second for V4.1 on the channel's DGX Spark is unmeasured; Unsloth's claim of up to 3x faster inference than other CPU/VRAM/ngram repos is their number, not ours.
suggested_outline:
Yesterday's beta: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, 552B parameters with about 16B active, now runs locally in about 125 GB at 1-bit with its Engram table on SSD
The catch: support means running -- no V4.1 fine-tuning recipe, notebook or memory figure shipped, and the smallest download is 233.0 GB
What you train tonight: the stock Unsloth QLoRA recipe -- 4-bit model, LoRA adapters, your question-answer dataset, export to GGUF -- on a model that fits your card
notes: Tool family: FireCrawl returned HTTP 402 (insufficient credits) on the single permitted test call, so discovery ran on web_search and reading on web_extract (fallback family); 6 searches and 9 page fetches spent, 9 sources cited. Angle check: 'the stock LoRA recipe is now one flag different' is NOT confirmed for fine-tuning. What v0.1.909-beta actually shipped for V4.1 is run support (Dynamic GGUFs from 233 GB, a run guide, a llama.cpp PR); the release's Training section is generic (FSDP2 multi-GPU), the guide's train bullet points at other models, and the notebook catalog has no V4/V4.1 entry -- so the brief corrects the angle to: run support shipped, the stock QLoRA recipe is unchanged and does not yet reach V4.1. The one-flag idea survives only as: in the stock recipe, swapping models IS one string (claim 8), but no 4-bit V4.1 training checkpoint exists to swap in. Conflict: DeepSeek's safetensors card metadata says 763B params, Unsloth's GGUF card says 748B params, and the release notes split it as 552B backbone plus 196B Engram; the brief uses Unsloth's split because it names the parts. Thin spots: all memory figures are for inference, none for training; the notebook-catalog absence is read from the README fetched 2026-10-20 and could lag the repo.
viewer_situation: You've got a 24 GB gaming GPU -- or a 128 GB DGX Spark -- you watched DeepSeek V4.1 land yesterday, and you want your own fine-tuned copy of it running tonight.
process_steps: Install Unsloth locally (pip install unsloth, or the one-line curl installer) on a Linux, WSL or Windows machine with an NVIDIA GPU.
Pick an instruct model that has a published 4-bit checkpoint and paste its name, like unsloth/llama-3.1-8b-unsloth-bnb-4bit, into the notebook's model cell.
Load the model with FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained and load_in_4bit = True for QLoRA.
Attach LoRA adapters with get_peft_model, leaving the base weights frozen.
Prepare a question-and-answer dataset (two columns), or generate one synthetically.
Train with the defaults (learning_rate = 2e-4, per_device_train_batch_size = 2, gradient_accumulation_steps = 4) and watch the loss fall toward 0.5 to 1.0.
Save the LoRA adapter, export to GGUF, and run it in Ollama, llama.cpp or LM Studio.
objection: Every LoRA adapter you train still sits on top of a 552B backbone whose smallest published download is 233.0 GB -- the adapter changes behavior, not the base model's footprint -- so fine-tuning V4.1 on consumer hardware is not something this release enables.
